analysis.one_liner: Makes illegal robocalls a federal crime and doubles fines for caller ID spoofing.
analysis.headline: Four senators proposed making illegal robocalling a federal crime with prison terms of up to 3 years, but the bill has sat in the Senate Commerce Committee since its introduction.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it a federal crime to knowingly violate the nation's robocall law — up to one year in prison, and up to three years for repeat offenders, mass-volume call operations, or fraud schemes. It would also double the maximum fine for deliberately faking caller ID from $10,000 to $20,000 per violation. It was introduced in December 2025 and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, where it has not moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone with a phone. Americans receive billions of illegal robocalls and scam texts each year, and older adults lose the most to phone fraud. The bill gives federal prosecutors a new tool — criminal charges, not just civil fines — against the operations that flood phones with unwanted and fraudulent calls, and raises the price of spoofing caller ID to trick people into answering.

how_it_helps.text: Makes willful and knowing violations of the Telephone Consumer Protection Act a federal crime for the first time: up to 1 year in prison, or up to 3 years for repeat offenders, operations sending over 100,000 autodialed calls a day (or 1 million a month), calls meant to further a felony, or calls causing $5,000 or more in losses.
The criminal penalty covers autodialed calls and prerecorded-voice calls, plus robotexts sent to mobile phones without the recipient's consent.
Doubles the maximum civil penalty for knowingly providing false caller ID information — the 'spoofing' trick used to make scam calls look local or official — from $10,000 to $20,000 per violation.

analysis.who_pays: Telemarketing companies, robocall operations, and text-blasting firms that knowingly break the robocall law. Compliant callers would face no new burden, since the criminal penalties apply only to willful and knowing violations. The cost to violators is fines of up to $20,000 per spoofed call and, in aggravated cases, prison time.
analysis.who_pays_short: Telemarketers who knowingly break robocall law

drawbacks.text: The prison terms are modest — 1 to 3 years — and the $20,000 cap per spoofing violation is small compared to what large robocall operations earn, so the bill may not change the economics of mass robocalling by itself.

Businesses that use autodialers legitimately, such as debt collectors and appointment-reminder services, would face criminal rather than just civil exposure if they get consent questions wrong; the bill softens this by applying criminal penalties only to 'willful and knowing' violations, but boundaries in this area of law have historically been disputed.
The bill adds penalties but no new enforcement funding or mandate, so its real-world effect depends on whether federal prosecutors choose to bring cases.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but modest: criminal liability is the strongest tool short of shutting operations down, and it targets only knowing violators, so compliant businesses are largely untouched. The design is narrower than the problem — large robocall operations are often overseas, anonymous, and reconstituted under new names, which prison terms for whoever can be caught will only partly address. It is a reasonable tightening of the law rather than a sweeping fix.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on December 4, 2025, and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, where it has sat with no further action while Congress remains in session.

narrative.text: Senator Catherine Cortez Masto introduced the bill on December 4, 2025, joined by Senators Klobuchar, Gillibrand, and King.
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote has occurred since; the committee has taken no further action on the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, nobody — the bill has only been referred to committee, so illegal robocall and spoofing operations continue to face the old penalty structure with no criminal exposure.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nobody yet; robocallers keep old rules

for.name: Catherine Cortez Masto
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its lead sponsor.

sides.party_line_note: Too early to tell: three senators (two Democrats and one independent) back it and no Republicans have signed on yet, and no votes have occurred.

industries.note: For the first time, knowingly violating the robocall law could mean federal prison, and spoofing caller ID could cost $20,000 per call instead of $10,000. Operators who comply with consent rules face little change; the burden falls on those flooding phones with unwanted and fraudulent calls.

These industries use the same autodialer technology the bill covers. Firms that stay within the law are unaffected, but those that misjudge consent requirements would now risk criminal charges on top of civil suits.

analysis.trajectory: Penalty bills like this one usually die quietly in the Senate Commerce Committee: no hearing has been scheduled, the cosponsor list is small (3), and no Republicans have signed on. Unless it is attached to a broader telecom or anti-fraud package, it will most likely sit in committee for the rest of the 119th Congress.
